what_it_does: Modern data centers are starting to use a technology called CXL (Compute Express Link) — a fast electrical connection that lets multiple computers share a single large pool of memory, rather than each machine needing its own private memory chips. When several computers (hosts) share that memory pool, they all need a local fast-memory buffer (a cache) to avoid re-fetching the same data from the shared pool over and over. The problem is that each host accesses the shared memory in its own unpredictable rhythm, and standard rules for deciding which data to keep in the cache (replacement and bypass policies) treat all hosts the same, making them a poor fit. Alchemy, the system proposed here, uses a reinforcement-learning agent — software that learns by trial and reward, like training a dog — to watch each host's individual access pattern separately and tune the cache decisions per host in real time. The learning signal comes from sampling how well each decision worked, measured per host, so the cache adapts as access patterns shift.
